title: Executing the Minority Attack
idea: The Carlsbad structure, and the plan that comes with it. You have two pawns against three on the queenside and you attack there anyway, because the goal is not material — it is to force a permanent weakness on c6 and then spend the rest of the game attacking it. Four moves, in a specific order, and none of them are tactics. This is what having a plan on move twelve actually looks like.

cues.text: White pawns on a2 and b2 against black pawns on a7, b7 and c6. Fewer pawns, attacking anyway.
The c-file is half open for you and Black's c6 pawn sits on it.
Black's pawn on d5 fixes the structure, so the weakness you create cannot be undone.

recognition.prompt: You have two queenside pawns against three. What are you playing for?

choices.text: To force a backward pawn on c6 by playing b4-b5
choices.why: Push b5 and Black must either take, leaving a backward c-pawn on a half-open file, or allow bxc6, which leaves the same weakness. It cannot be repaired by a pawn, so it is a target for the rest of the game.

choices.text: To win a pawn on the queenside
choices.why: You are outnumbered there. Material is not the goal — the structural concession is.
That is Black's plan in this structure, not yours. Your play is on the other wing.

choices.text: To trade everything and reach an endgame
choices.why: The endgame is where the weakness pays off, but you have to create it first.

plan.goal: Prepare b4 with a3, then push b4-b5 to hit c6.
Put a rook on b1 before pushing, so the file opens onto something.
Do not open the centre — the frozen d5 pawn is what makes the weakness permanent.

line.threat: Nothing is threatened by either side. This is the moment club players drift and strong players start a plan.
hints: Your play is on the queenside, and it starts with a pawn you have not moved.
You want b4 next, but it needs support first.

moves.why: The quiet start. It supports b4 so the pawn cannot be met by a piece landing there, and it commits to nothing else.
Black regroups toward the kingside, which is where his counterplay lives.
The minority advances. Next comes b5, and Black cannot stop it with pawns without creating a different weakness.
Black brings the knight toward the kingside.

hints: Before the final push, put a piece behind it.
Which file are you about to open?

moves.why: The rook takes the file before it opens. This is the move club players skip, and it is the difference between a plan and a pawn push.
Black eyes the kingside and waits.
There it is. Whatever Black does, c6 ends up backward on a half-open file with your rook already looking at it.

terminal.summary: Four quiet moves and Black has a weakness that cannot be repaired for the rest of the game. Notice what you did not do: no tactics, no calculation, no attack on the king. You looked at the pawn structure, identified the one concession you could force, and spent four moves forcing it. That is the whole skill. The follow-up is mechanical — trade off the defenders, double on the c-file, and win the pawn or the endgame it produces.

mistakes.why: Breaking in the centre throws away the entire plan. The frozen d5 pawn is what makes c6 a permanent target — release the tension and Black's pieces come alive and there is no weakness to attack.

moves.why: Rook first is also fine. The order of a3 and Rb1 is flexible; what matters is that both happen before b4-b5.
A reasonable developing move that does not advance the plan. In a position with no tactics, a move that does not serve the plan is a wasted move.

spot.prompt: Tap the pawn you are going to make permanently weak.
spot.why: Push b4-b5 and c6 becomes backward on a half-open file — it cannot advance, and no pawn can defend it. That target is what the whole minority attack exists to create.
